sections.body: This submersible filter does mechanical, chemical and biological filtration and also circulates the water. The flow is adjustable, and it suits tanks up to about 100 litres. Because it sits inside the tank it needs no plumbing, which makes it a good first filter or a second filter for a tank that needs extra circulation.

The media basket lifts out for rinsing, which takes a couple of minutes each month. Rinse the foam and the bio media in a bucket of tank water, never under the tap, and replace only the carbon, which wears out within weeks. Keep the intake clear of plants and, for shrimp or fry, cover it with a [pre-filter sponge](/product/intake-pre-filter-sponge-9pack).

Planted tanks and fish such as bettas prefer gentle flow. Turn the dial down until the surface moves a little and plant leaves sway, and aim the outlet along the back or side glass. A rolling surface also helps oxygen reach the water, so do not turn it down so far that the surface goes still.

sections.h: A small filter for small tanks
sections.body: This compact filter sits inside the tank and cleans, circulates and oxygenates at once. It is a good fit for small tanks, quarantine tubs and hospital setups, where plumbing is a nuisance and flow needs to stay gentle. It has no hoses to hide and no space is needed outside the tank.

Rinse the sponge in tank water when the flow drops, and never in tap water. If the sponge is the only biological surface, move it carefully and replace it only when it is falling apart. For a quarantine tank it helps to keep a spare sponge running in your main tank, so that it already carries bacteria when you need it.

Reverse osmosis removes most dissolved minerals, leaving very soft water. That is the starting point for soft-water tanks, shrimp and discus, where tap water is too hard or has too many dissolved solids. This countertop unit has sediment and carbon stages followed by an RO membrane, and connects to a tap.

sections.h: RO water is not ready to use
sections.body: Pure RO water has almost no minerals, which fish, shrimp and plants need. Remineralise it to the hardness your animals want before adding it to a tank, or blend it with tap water to lower the hardness a little. Test the result with an [EC meter](/product/ph-ec-meter-4in1) or [GH and KH strips](/product/gh-kh-test-strips-7in1) before it goes in.

An RO system makes wastewater alongside the clean water, and the ratio varies by pressure and membrane, so collect the waste for plants or cleaning. Replace the sediment and carbon stages and the membrane on the schedule that comes with the unit. As the membrane ages, the water gets harder, so check the output with the EC meter regularly.

A brushless USB-powered gravel vacuum that pulls waste from the substrate without a hand pump. The V2 motor moves water faster, and an intake guard keeps shrimp and fry out of the stream. You power it from a USB supply, so you can use a power bank or a charger.

sections.h: Using it in a planted tank
sections.body: Hover just above the substrate and let the waste lift, rather than digging into root zones. Over [aqua soil](/product/aqua-soil-planted-substrate) especially, stay on the surface so the granules do not get pulled up. Run the drained water into a bucket or a drain, and refill with treated water.
Rinse the unit in clean water after use, and keep the electronics dry. Do not run it dry. Check the guard for debris after each use, since a blocked intake reduces suction.

sections.h: Vacuum and drain in one pass
sections.body: This battery-powered siphon has a gravel head that vacuums the substrate and drains water in the same motion. It is intended for tanks up to about 90 litres, which suits most home tanks. Because it is battery-powered there is no priming and no hand pump, so water-change day is faster.

Work in sections, pushing the head into the gravel and lifting as the debris swirls up, and keep going until about a quarter to a third of the water is out. In a planted tank skip the root zones. Treat the new water with [conditioner](/product/water-conditioner-100ml) before you refill the tank.
Charge or replace the batteries before you start, since a half-finished water change is a nuisance. Keep the battery housing dry and rinse the gravel head after use.

An electric pump-and-hose system that drains the tank and refills it straight from the tap. A water change that used to be a bucket-and-backache routine becomes a five-minute job, which makes it more likely you will do it weekly.

Tap water contains chlorine or chloramine, which harm fish and bacteria. When you refill directly from the tap, add [conditioner](/product/water-conditioner-100ml) to the tank for the volume of water you are adding, either before or while it fills. Match the temperature to the tank by feel or with a [thermometer strip](/product/stick-on-thermometer-strips), and fill slowly so that fish are not stressed by a sudden change.

Direct the inflow onto a plate, rock or your hand to avoid blowing substrate around. Never leave the tank filling unattended, and make sure the drain hose end is secure in a sink or outside. Rinse the hoses afterwards.

This air-driven device lifts debris from the substrate without swallowing the substrate itself, which is a common problem with powerful siphons over fine sand or [aqua soil](/product/aqua-soil-planted-substrate). It is a simple, cheap tool that works as a sand washer and, with a hose, as a water changer.

It runs from an air pump, so you need a pump, airline tubing and a spare outlet. A [dual-outlet pump](/product/dual-outlet-air-pump) leaves one outlet free for the tank's filter. Check the tubing fits before you start.

Hold the device just above the surface of the substrate and let the air lift the waste. Work slowly across the tank in sections. If it pulls up substrate, lift it a little or reduce the air. Catch the waste water in a bucket and refill with treated water.

These 30 cm tweezers are brushed stainless with fine tips that grip delicate stems without crushing them. The length keeps your knuckles dry in deep tanks and lets you plant in a crowded foreground without disturbing the neighbours.

Grip a stem low, near the base, and push it into the substrate at a slight angle. Release the tweezers as you pull them out, so that the plant stays put. For several stems, plant them in small groups spaced a finger apart, and use [plant weights](/product/plant-weights-10pk) on loose cuttings until they root.

Rinse with clean water and dry the tweezers after use. Stainless will resist rust, but a tool left wet in a drawer can spot. Pair them with [spring scissors](/product/curved-spring-scissors) for trimming.

sections.h: A bar for a 40 cm tank
sections.body: This is a 40 cm full-spectrum bar tuned for planted tanks, with strong reds for colour and balanced whites for growth. The aluminium body runs cool, and it fits both rimless and framed tanks. Choose it for a tank around 40 cm long. For longer tanks, use a longer bar, such as the [Aurora 48](/product/aurora-48-planted-tank-led).

Put it on a plug-in timer and start with about six hours a day. Increase slowly if plants are growing and the glass stays clear. If algae appears, shorten the day before changing anything else. A bar that is too bright for the plants is a common cause of algae in a new tank.

Treat a bar like this as a low to medium light. It suits anubias, java fern, cryptocoryne, mosses and many stem plants kept near the surface. Demanding carpet plants are better matched to a brighter fixture and CO2.

sections.h: A small light for small jobs
sections.body: A tiny clamp-on spotlight for nano tanks, shrimp bowls and plant corners. Clip it to the rim, aim it at the plants and plug it in. It is a handy supplement for a dim corner and a simple light for a small desktop setup.

A spotlight this small lights a small area. It suits low-light plants such as anubias, java fern and moss, and floating plants. For a bigger tank or demanding plants, use a full bar such as the [clip-on nano grow light](/product/clip-on-nano-grow-light) or the [40 cm bar](/product/full-spectrum-led-40cm). Run it on a timer for about six to seven hours a day.

This pen reads pH, EC, TDS and temperature in one probe. Unlike a [basic pH pen](/product/digital-ph-pen-meter), which reads pH only, it can also tell you how many dissolved solids are in the water. For planted-tank dosing and RO top-ups, that gives you a number to watch.

EC and TDS rise as you add fertiliser or minerals, and fall with water changes of softer water. Track the number over time, rather than chasing a single value. In a shrimp tank, use it to check remineralised [RO water](/product/ro-countertop-3-stage) before it goes in. TDS is calculated from EC, so different meters may read differently.

Calibrate the pH and the EC with fresh solution when you first use it and at regular intervals afterwards. Rinse the probe in clean water between samples and keep it clean. A dirty or dry probe drifts.

sections.h: The first thing into every bucket
sections.body: Tap water usually contains chlorine or chloramine, which kill fish gills and filter bacteria. This conditioner neutralises both immediately. The 100 ml bottle treats roughly 2,000 litres of water, so it lasts a long time in a typical home tank.

Dose for the volume of new water you add, following the label, either into the bucket or into the tank as it fills. If you fill straight from the tap with an [electric water exchanger](/product/electric-water-exchanger), dose the tank for the volume being added. Dosing a little for the whole tank is safer than guessing low.

A conditioner makes tap water safe against chlorine and chloramine. It does not cure an ammonia spike, and it does not replace testing. Check the water with [test strips](/product/test-strips-8-in-1-100-count) after a water change if livestock look stressed.
These slow-dissolve clarifying tablets are used when water is green or cloudy. Dose according to the label, keep the filter running and watch the tank clear over a few days.

Cloudy water usually comes from a bacterial bloom in a new tank, overfeeding or a heavily cleaned filter. Green water comes from too much light or nutrients. A tablet clears the symptom, but without a change the water can turn again. Shorten the light period, feed less and check fertiliser dosing in a planted tank.
Clumped particles end up in the filter, so rinse the sponge or replace the [floss pad](/product/aquarium-filter-floss-pad) after the water clears. Do a water change if the tank is heavily stocked.

These ceramic hides are sized for shrimp and bottom dwellers. Berried females find cover, moulting shrimp have a safe place to harden, and biofilm grows on the glazed surface for grazing. The natural clay look sits quietly in any scape.

Place one or two caves on the substrate, partly covered with moss or leaf litter, rather than in the open. Shrimp feel safer under cover. Rinse before use, and leave the biofilm alone, since it is food. A cave also suits small bottom-dwelling fish that like a shelter.

sections.h: When live plants will not cooperate
sections.body: This is a low-maintenance artificial plant set for tanks where live plants do not suit, for example in dim tanks or with fish that eat or uproot plants. It has weighted bases, soft-edged leaves and no paint bleed.

Place the plants in groups of different heights, with the tallest at the back, and leave swimming space. Check that edges are smooth enough for long-finned fish, and rinse the set before use. Clean the leaves with a soft brush when algae builds up, and consider mixing in a few live plants, such as [anubias or java fern on wood](/product/natural-driftwood-branch), which tolerate low light.

sections.h: A wreck that doubles as a cave
sections.body: A detailed resin wreck with openings that work as a cave network for cichlids and catfish. It is non-toxic and weighted, so it stays put on the substrate, and it looks better with a bit of algae on it.

Rinse it before use, and check that fish can swim out of every opening without getting stuck. Place it on a flat patch of substrate, or in the sand, away from the filter intake. Secure it so that digging fish cannot undermine it.
A live bacterial cleaner that helps break down sludge and mulm in gravel and filters. Dose it weekly, according to the label, and the bacteria work on organic waste between water changes.

It does not remove waste that physically sits on the substrate, so keep up regular siphoning with a [gravel siphon](/product/gravel-siphon-kit) and rinse filter media in tank water. It works best in a tank that is not overfed and is kept steady. If you see sludge building in a tank that is already well maintained, reduce feeding first.
A water quality stabiliser designed to buffer swings between water changes, for steadier pH and calmer fish. The dose is one cap per 40 litres at each water change.

A stabiliser helps, but it does not replace testing. If the tank's pH or hardness is moving, look for the cause, such as heavy feeding, a dying plant, CO2 or low KH. Test with [strips](/product/gh-kh-test-strips-7in1) before and after a water change, and keep a record. Do not overdose to try to fix a problem.
A hand-blown glass ornament that catches the light in a way plastic never will. Each piece is one of a kind, so yours will differ from the photo in shape and colour.

Rinse it in clean water before use, and place it where it catches the light without being in the path of fish that dash. Glass can chip, so check the edges after handling and remove the ornament if it cracks. Keep it away from strong flow, where it could roll.
A resting turtle ornament for riverbank layouts. It is hollow underneath, so it also works as a hide for bottom dwellers such as corydoras or small catfish.

Rinse and place it on the substrate, partly buried, near plants and rock so that it looks like part of the scape. Make sure there is an opening large enough for the fish to enter and leave. Algae will grow on it over time and can be brushed off.
